skills.name: Channel discounts and promotions
skills.status: team decision — default discounts stated by Fede 2026-10-09 (pricing sheet); the Vrbo opt-out is approved in the Hub knowledge base
skills.tools: PriceLabs, PMS, Airbnb and Vrbo dashboards.
skills.whenToUse: setting or reviewing stay-length discounts, Airbnb's top-rated-guest discount, or Vrbo promotions.
skills.summary: Default Airbnb discounts are weekly 24%, monthly 28%, trip length 21–26%, early bird 20%, last minute 20%; the 15% top-rated-guest discount is a per-listing choice (encouraged after slow bookings, paired with a 55% markup); opt out of Vrbo Members Only Deals.

sections.title: Steps
sections.markdown:
1. **Vrbo Members Only Deals** (host-funded 12–20%, stacked on weekly/monthly discounts from 2026-09-18): opt out. The control location depends on the setup (Vrbo direct, Hospitable, Hostaway).
2. **Airbnb top-rated-guest discount** (15%, guests rated 4.8+ with 3+ reviews): a per-listing choice. When we use it, the Airbnb markup is 55% instead of 44% ([[skills/ota-markup]]). We encourage it for listings coming out of slow bookings, for an extra exposure bump in Airbnb search (Fede, 2026-10-09; Spencer's two listings). Keep a per-client opt-out: some clients refuse it, others want it only with a markup.
3. **Default Airbnb discounts** (Fede's pricing sheet, 2026-10-09; set in PriceLabs):
   - Weekly (7+ nights) 24%; monthly (28+ nights) 28%.
   - Trip length: 3+ nights 21%, 5+ nights 22%, 14+ nights 26%.
   - Early bird (booked 1+ month ahead) 20%; last minute (0–28 days ahead) 20%.

sections.title: How Airbnb stacks them (checked 2026-10-09)
sections.markdown:
- Only one of these applies to a reservation: new listing promotion, custom promotion, length of stay (weekly, monthly, trip length), early bird, last minute. Airbnb picks by priority in that order, not by size.
- The top-rated-guest discount (15%) is the one that adds on top of whichever applies; it is taken off the already-discounted price.
- A non-refundable discount, if offered, comes off last, after all other discounts.
- With our defaults, trip length starts at 3 nights (21%) and outranks early bird and last minute, so those two only reach stays under 3 nights.
- Common client question. Answer: "Only one of weekly, monthly, trip length, early bird or last minute applies, picked by Airbnb's order; the top-rated-guest discount is the only one that adds on top."

sections.title: Do not
sections.markdown:
- Do not leave a promotion on that a client did not choose: log a client's choice to keep one in Assembly.
- Do not stack discounts without checking the effective nightly rate (see [[skills/ota-markup]]).

sections.title: Decided / open
sections.markdown:
- Decided: default discounts and the two Airbnb markups, 44% without and 55% with the top-rated-guest discount (Fede, 2026-10-09). They replace the 2026-09-10 private-note figures (weekly was noted as 25%).
- Open: Fede's review of the page as a whole.

skills.name: Comp analysis (fit, tier, performance)
skills.owner: Fede approves comp sets and any number sent to a client or lead.
skills.channels: Airbnb first (search and calendars); AirDNA and PriceLabs market data.
skills.tools: RM (fit engine, coverage, AirDNA discovery), AirDNA, PriceLabs Market Dashboard.
skills.whenToUse: client pricing setup, lead analysis, purchase underwriting, new-build estimates, and checking a client's own comps.
skills.summary: Judge every comp on three separate checks (fit, competitive tier, performance); only comps that pass fit and sit in the subject's tier or above may set rate targets or ceilings.

sections.title: Steps
sections.markdown:
1. **Fit:** same product for the same guests and trip (rooms, amenities, location, design, signature).
2. **Competitive tier:** reputation and presentation (Guest Favorite, rating, reviews, Superhost, photos, search position).
3. **Performance:** what the comp books and asks, always labeled booked or asking.
4. Gate out mid-term rentals (28+ night minimums) and anything that fails bedrooms, capacity, class, or marketed amenities.

Full method: [[playbooks/comp-analysis]] and RM `docs/comp-analyzer-v3.md`.

sections.title: Do not
sections.markdown:
- Do not let one blended score decide a comp.
- Do not let a high-fit but weak-tier comp set a ceiling.
- Do not treat a lead (city page card, AirDNA row) as an approved comp.

skills.name: Comps with a different guest count
skills.status: stated in meetings — Fede's method across calls (2026-08 to 2026-10); flagged by Fede as very important 2026-10-09
skills.channels: Airbnb first (search filters by party size); PriceLabs comp filters.
skills.tools: Airbnb and PriceLabs comp filters (bedrooms, bathrooms, guests), RM comp scorecard, booking history by party size.
skills.whenToUse: any comp review, and whenever a client sends a comp that hosts a different number of guests than their listing.
skills.summary: Compare against comps with the same real guest capacity first; a comp that hosts fewer or more guests is context, not a rate setter, because capacity changes who books, which searches it appears in, and the revenue tier.

sections.title: Steps
sections.markdown:
1. Build tiers by capacity and layout: Tier 1 matches bedrooms, guest capacity, bed setup, layout, and indoor gathering space; Tier 2 keeps the rooms with different amenities; Tier 3 is market context ([[skills/comp-analysis]]; capacity within ±20%).
2. Filter comps by guest count in Airbnb or PriceLabs, and compare pacing and occupancy, not just the displayed nightly rate.
3. Treat a comp with a different guest count as context only. Ticket #12: the client's "best comp" is the same unit as hers, but it hosts 4 and hers hosts 6, so it sells to a different party size.
4. Price for the party size the listing actually books, not its maximum. In a Colorado case, pricing a home for 14 guests hurt ranking because real demand was 6–10 guests (guest avatar mismatch).
5. Set a different capacity's revenue target from comps at that capacity, not from a fixed amount per extra guest: a 7-guest home was estimated at about $70K a year, 14-guest comps at $90K–$150K, and an 8-guest comp with a sauna at about $99K. Check the permit or HOA occupancy limit before changing listed capacity.
6. Before setting extra-guest fees, look at booking history by party size and booking type to find the valuable group segments.

sections.title: Do not
sections.markdown:
- Do not carry a comp's rate across capacities with a per-guest uplift.
- Do not assume a higher maximum occupancy is better.

sections.title: Decided / open
sections.markdown: - Open: no standard capacity adjustment or extra-guest-fee rule is on file. Fede's message to Michelle on guest-count comps (2026-10-09) was not captured by the Hub: add it here.

skills.name: Explaining markups and discounts to a client
skills.status: team decision — Fede's message to Spencer, 2026-10-09
skills.owner: Fede (wording). The account owner sends it.
skills.tools: Airbnb listing discounts page, PMS listing markups (e.g. Hospitable), PriceLabs target rate.
skills.whenToUse: after onboarding sets markups and discounts, or when a client asks why Airbnb shows discounts, whether discounts stack, or why the Airbnb price is higher than PriceLabs.
skills.summary: Explain in one short message that PriceLabs sets the target, the channel markup (Airbnb 44% or 55%) absorbs fees and discounts, only one of length-of-stay, early bird or last minute applies, and the top-rated-guest discount is the one that stacks; show one worked example.

sections.title: Steps
sections.markdown:
1. Check the live settings first: each listing's Airbnb and Vrbo markup in the PMS, and the discounts on Airbnb's discounts page. Never send numbers you have not seen on the listing.
2. Fill the template below. Say which markup each listing uses and why: 44% without the top-rated-guest discount, 55% with it. For listings coming out of slow bookings, say we turned the discount on for an extra exposure bump ([[skills/channel-discounts]]).
3. Keep the stacking explanation to two sentences ([[skills/channel-discounts]], "How Airbnb stacks them").
4. Use one worked example: a $100 target, or the listing's own target if the client prefers real numbers.
5. Add the taxes line only if pass-through taxes were set up ([[skills/taxes-pass-through]]).

sections.title: Message template
sections.markdown:
**Your target rate and the markup**

PriceLabs sets your target nightly rate. Each channel adds a markup on top, so platform fees and discounts come out of the markup, not your target. Vrbo is [12]%.

On Airbnb we use one of two markups: **44%** when we don't use the top-rated-guest discount, **55%** when we do. [Reason, e.g.: Since your listings are coming out of a slow booking period, we turned on the top-rated-guest discount for an extra exposure bump in Airbnb search, so your listings are at 55%.]

**Your Airbnb discounts**

- Trip length: [21]% for 3+ nights, [22]% for 5+, [26]% for 14+
- Weekly (7+ nights): [24]%
- Monthly (28+ nights): [28]%
- Early bird (booked 1+ month ahead): [20]%
- Last minute (booked within 28 days): [20]%
- Top-rated guests (rated 4.8+ with 3+ reviews): [15]%

**How they combine**

Only one of the length-of-stay, early-bird or last-minute discounts applies to a booking. Airbnb picks length of stay first, so early bird and last minute only matter on 1–2 night stays. The top-rated-guest discount is the only one that adds on top.

**Example:** with a $100 PriceLabs target, Airbnb shows $155. A 7-night stay gets the weekly discount: $117.80 a night. A top-rated guest gets 15% more off: $100.13, right at your target. These are nightly prices before Airbnb's fees and taxes.

[If set up: **Taxes are separate:** the county taxes we set up show at checkout and come to you as their own "pass-through" payout line.]

sections.title: Example math (55% markup, $100 target, defaults)
sections.markdown:
- 2 nights, booked 2 months out: early bird 20%, $124.00 (top-rated guest $105.40).
- 3 nights: trip length 21% outranks early bird, $122.45 (top-rated $104.08).
- 7 nights: weekly 24%, $117.80 (top-rated $100.13).
- 30 nights: monthly 28%, $111.60 (top-rated $94.86, a bit under target on purpose).
- With 44% (no top-rated discount): 7 nights is $144 × 0.76 = $109.44.

sections.title: Do not
sections.markdown:
- Do not promise that a discount brings bookings or a ranking position: say "exposure bump", not a result.
- Do not quote a payout after Airbnb's fees: our numbers are guest-facing nightly prices before fees and taxes.
- Do not send a client another client's numbers.

sections.title: Decided / open
sections.markdown:
- Decided: two Airbnb markups, 44% and 55% (Fede, 2026-10-09). Spencer's listings: both at 55%, Vrbo 12%.
- Open: Fede's review of the Hub article `airbnb-discounts-and-markups`.

skills.name: International taxes (Mexico first)
skills.status: draft — from Fede's questions to Michelle Lohr on Hub ticket #84 (2026-10-09); Mexico details pending Fede
skills.owner: Fede. The owner's accountant confirms what is owed.
skills.channels: Airbnb first; check Vrbo and Booking.com per country.
skills.tools: the owner's payout breakdown (screenshot), the channel's tax settings for that country.
skills.whenToUse: any listing outside the US, or an owner who is a tax resident of another country.
skills.summary: Abroad, the platform may withhold income tax and VAT from the host's payout as well as charge taxes to the guest; separate the two, work out the owner's net per night, and use it for the price floor.

sections.title: Why it differs from the US
sections.markdown:
- In the US, local taxes are mostly charged to the guest; the fix is collecting the missing ones as pass-through ([[skills/taxes-pass-through]]).
- Abroad, the platform may also take taxes from the host's payout. For a host resident in Mexico, Fede's understanding (to confirm with the owner): Airbnb withholds income tax and VAT from the payout. Those lower what the owner nets per night, which is why Michelle asked for a slow-season price floor (ticket #84).
- Tax residency changes the treatment: Michelle is a resident of Mexico (ticket #84, 2026-10-09).

sections.title: Steps
sections.markdown:
1. Ask the owner for their tax residency, every tax they pay locally, and a payout breakdown. Fede's opening question: "Are there other taxes you are paying locally besides VAT on accommodation and the lodging tax?"
2. Separate taxes charged to the guest (collected at checkout) from taxes withheld from the host (taken from the payout).
3. Check which guest taxes the channel collects and remits, and add any missing one as pass-through ([[skills/taxes-pass-through]]).
4. Work out the owner's net per night after withholdings and channel fees, and feed it into [[skills/minimum-price-floor]].
5. Record each country's confirmed rules in a section below, with the date and source.

sections.title: Mexico (as of 2026-10-09, to confirm)
sections.markdown:
- Guest-side: VAT on accommodation; Impuesto Sobre Hospedaje (state lodging tax), 6% per Fede's message.
- Host-side: Airbnb withholds income tax and VAT from a Mexico-resident host's payout (Fede's question; the owner's confirmation pending).
- Withholding rates: not on file.

sections.title: Do not
sections.markdown:
- Do not assume the US pass-through setup covers taxes withheld from the payout.
- Do not give tax or legal advice: revenue advice only; the owner's accountant confirms.

sections.title: Decided / open
sections.markdown: - Open: Fede to confirm Mexico's rates and rules; add other countries as they come up.

skills.name: Visibility recovery after a mid-term stay
skills.status: draft — method from Fede's answer on Hub ticket #12, gaps answered 2026-10-09
skills.owner: Fede (method). Andrés applies the rates; Martín uses the client wording.
skills.channels: mostly Airbnb (its ranking leans on conversion). Vrbo and Booking.com: case by case.
skills.tools: PriceLabs (rates), RankBreeze (visibility and conversion), the guest's MTR booking.
skills.whenToUse: a client asks why a listing gets few views, ranks low, or is "not visible", and the listing has a mid-term stay (MTR, about 30+ nights) coming up, running, or just ended. Also when planning rates around a confirmed MTR.
skills.summary: After a mid-term stay, relaunch the listing like a new launch (competitive rates for 30 days of open calendar) to rebuild Airbnb conversion and ranking, without undercutting a possible extension.

sections.title: Why it happens
sections.markdown:
- During an MTR, Airbnb records no new short-stay bookings for the listing for weeks.
- Conversion (search views that turn into bookings) is one of Airbnb's strongest ranking signals. With no recent conversions, the listing comes back ranked lower.

sections.title: Steps
sections.markdown:
1. **Before the MTR:** keep competitive rates on the open dates before check-in, so the listing keeps converting until the stay starts.
2. **While an extension is possible:** hold the rates for dates after check-out where they are. A guest who is thinking about extending must not see lower rates on Airbnb.
3. **Extension check:** propose asking the MTR guest about an extension about 4 weeks before check-out (ticket #12: early April for a May check-out). That is the first proposal; adjust the timing to the client's response.
4. **After check-out, no extension:** treat the return like a new listing launch ([[skills/new-listing-launch]]). Use competitive rates for the first 30 days of open calendar after the stay, to win bookings fast, rebuild conversion, and regain ranking.
   - "Competitive" has no fixed number: set it from a separate analysis of where the market is at the time (comps, market occupancy and rates for those dates).
5. **After the 30 days:** step rates back up based on pickup and pacing, plus visibility and conversion against the market (check in [[stack/rankbreeze]]).
6. **Tell the client** in this shape: a bold "<property> visibility" title; the cause in two sentences (algorithm, conversion); the key idea (relaunch like a new listing); the plan split "Before the MTR stay" / "After the MTR stay"; the dated next step (the extension check).

sections.title: Do not
sections.markdown:
- Do not promise a ranking position or a date when visibility comes back.
- Do not lower rates on dates the MTR guest could extend into before the extension is ruled out.
- Do not use this when there is no MTR: low visibility can also come from blocks, minimum stays, reviews, or listing quality. Check those first.

sections.title: Decided / open
sections.markdown:
- Decided by Fede (2026-10-09): relaunch level has no fixed % or floor (a separate market analysis sets it each time); the extension check is first proposed about 4 weeks before check-out and adjusted to the client's response; rates step back up by pickup, pacing, and RankBreeze visibility and conversion; mostly Airbnb.
- Open: Fede's review of this page as a whole.

skills.name: New listing launch pricing
skills.status: team decision — 2026-06-11 launch markup; the rest stated in meetings (Evidence v2)
skills.channels: Airbnb (the new-listing discount is Airbnb's); the competitive-first-weeks rule applies to every channel.
skills.whenToUse: a listing goes live for the first time, or comes back after a long gap (see [[skills/mtr-visibility-recovery]]).
skills.summary: Launch only when the listing is fully ready, price competitively for the first 30–60 days to win bookings and reviews, and offset Airbnb's new-listing discount with a 20% markup that steps down.

sections.title: Steps
sections.markdown:
1. Go live only when the listing is 100% ready, with professional photos.
2. Price competitively for the first 30–60 calendar days to win bookings and reviews. Far-out dates can carry a premium.
3. Airbnb gives new listings a 20% discount for the first guests. Mark base rates up 20% from day 1, drop the markup to 10% after 30 days out, and remove it after the first 3 bookings.
4. Price new or renovated properties to market potential and last year's market pacing, not to the owner's prior-year numbers ([[skills/no-history-pricing]]).

sections.title: Do not
sections.markdown:
- Do not launch an unfinished listing to "test the market".
- Do not lock in low rates on far-out peak dates during the launch window (one client opened 45 days out at a 20% discount to avoid locking low holiday rates).

sections.title: Decided / open
sections.markdown:
- Decided: the launch markup applies from day 1 on every new listing ([[decisions/2026-06-11-new-listing-launch-markup]]).
- Open: how "competitive" is set in numbers (see the market-analysis note in [[skills/mtr-visibility-recovery]]).

skills.name: Pricing a property without booking history
skills.status: stated in meetings — Evidence v2; a standard is still open
skills.tools: PriceLabs, market data (last year's market pacing), comps.
skills.whenToUse: new, renovated, or newly onboarded properties with no usable history of their own.
skills.summary: Price to market potential using last year's market pacing, set a 12-month revenue target by month, and review pacing quarterly.

sections.title: Steps
sections.markdown:

skills.name: Local taxes as pass-through, not markup
skills.status: stated in meetings — Fede's method on the Spencer onboarding call 2026-10-05; in use on Spencer's two listings and Fede's own Grand Prairie house
skills.owner: Fede. The team sets it up during onboarding; the owner and their accountant file and pay.
skills.channels: Airbnb (host-submitted taxes); Vrbo (check what it collects; with Hospitable payments, Hospitable is merchant of record).
skills.tools: Airbnb listing tax settings, Vrbo tax settings, the county or city tax rules, the owner's payout history.
skills.whenToUse: onboarding a listing, or when an owner says they pay a local occupancy, lodging, or tourism tax "out of profits".
skills.summary: Collect every local tax the channel does not remit as a separate pass-through tax at checkout, so the owner stops paying it from profit and the search price stays competitive; never mark up rates to cover tax.

sections.title: Why
sections.markdown:
- Guests see taxes only at checkout, not in search prices. A tax added as a separate line keeps the nightly rate competitive.
- Marking up the rate to cover a tax makes the listing less competitive, and the markup is revenue that is taxed again: the owner always loses.
- On Spencer's listings this moved about $100+ per booking out of the owner's profit and onto the guest (Fede's estimate on the call).

sections.title: Steps
sections.markdown:
1. List every tax the stay owes for the property's address: state, county, and city occupancy, lodging, transient, or tourism taxes, with the rate and any long-stay exemption (Bullitt County, KY: 4%, stays under 30 nights only).
2. Check what each channel already collects and remits. It differs by channel and jurisdiction: on Spencer's Mount Washington home, Vrbo collected 2 state taxes and the county tax, while Airbnb collected only the 2 state taxes.
3. For each tax the channel does not remit, add it to the listing as a tax the host submits (Airbnb: "taxes you will submit"), with the owner's registration or tax number for that authority. Airbnb collects it from the guest at checkout and pays it to the host as a separate payout line ("pass-through TOT" or "TLT").
4. Split a multi-part local tax into separate lines for tracking (Shelby County, KY: 3% transient room tax + 1% conference center tax), even when Airbnb shows them as one line.
5. Tell the owner and their accountant: the pass-through line is tax to remit, not revenue. They keep filing as before; only the source of the money changes.

sections.title: Do not
sections.markdown:
- Do not mark up nightly rates to cover taxes.
- Do not add a tax the channel already remits (the guest would pay it twice).
- Do not copy owners' tax ID or registration numbers into this vault or into tickets.
- Do not give tax or legal advice: we set up collection; the owner's accountant confirms what is owed.

# RevFactor Listing Review Digest

## What this skill does

When Fede shares a Rankbreeze Listing Review export, produce a digest that:

1. Reads the spreadsheet correctly (handles the Rankbreeze column structure)
2. Detects whether the listing is in its first year on platform (STLY = 0)
3. Computes ADR (not provided in the export — derive it from RevPAR / Occupancy)
4. Compares listing performance to market across RevPAR, ADR, and Occupancy
5. Renders a three-chart visual using `visualize:show_widget` for sharing with the owner
6. Surfaces the strategic narrative: what the data says about RevFactor's pricing strategy
7. On request, generates a polished owner-facing PDF report (see Step 8)

## Background on Fede's workflow

Fede is co-founder of two related businesses:

- **Blackbird** — full-service property management. Blackbird controls everything: listing copy, photos, pricing, guest comms, reviews, ops. Performance conversations can span the full operating picture because everything is in scope.
- **RevFactor** — revenue management strategy only. RevFactor's deliverable is the pricing strategy; the owner (or a separate operator) controls listing quality, photos, guest experience, reviews, and ops. Performance conversations must stay inside RevFactor's actual scope — revenue, RevPAR, ADR, occupancy, market positioning. RevFactor does not take credit for, or accept blame for, anything outside the pricing system.

RevFactor's pricing strategy is proprietary IP — it intentionally optimizes for **RevPAR** (revenue per available night) by holding **ADR** at a premium, accepting **lower occupancy** as the tradeoff. The owner conversation almost always lands on "why is my occupancy below market?" — and the answer is in the RevPAR and ADR numbers.

This skill should support that framing: lead with RevPAR, then ADR (the strategy executing), then occupancy (the deliberate tradeoff). Pricing strategy itself is never debated on calls; the data is.

### Identify the client type before drafting owner-facing materials

Before producing any owner-facing material (email draft, PDF report, talking points), identify whether the property is a Blackbird or RevFactor client. If unclear, ask Fede directly with a one-line question — don't guess. The answer changes the scope, the credit assignment, and the language.

**For Blackbird clients** — full scope is fair game. Listing performance, reviews, photo quality, guest experience, ops, channel mix, and pricing are all things "we" did and are accountable for. Plural-possessive language ("our listing," "our reviews," "what we delivered") is natural.

**For RevFactor clients** — scope is pricing strategy and revenue outcomes only. Adjust language accordingly:

- Don't take credit for things outside pricing. If the owner mentions reviews, photos, listing quality, growth post-relaunch, or anything operational — acknowledge it as theirs, not ours. "Glad to see the review score where it is — your team has nailed the guest experience" rather than "our reviews are strong."
- Don't say "our property" or "our listing." Use "the listing," "Emberglow," "your property."
- Don't take blame for things outside pricing either. If a listing underperforms because of photos, broken hot tub, or weak reviews, name it as an operational input we'd flag — not something we own.
- Credit on revenue outcomes stays with the strategy: "RevPAR is running 2.5x the comp set — the strategy is executing well" is fine. "We delivered a great spring" is not.
- Talking about future direction, use "the plan from here" or "what we'd watch next" rather than "what we'll do next" if "what we'll do" implies operational levers.

Owner-facing PDFs follow the same rules: the Blackbird version of the report can speak to listing quality and reviews; the RevFactor version stays scoped to revenue, rate, and occupancy.

## The Rankbreeze export structure

Files are typically named `Listing_Review_*.xlsx` with one client per file. Expect these columns:

- `Group Name` — the client/listing name
- `Year & Month` — e.g., "2026-01 (Jan)"
- `Rental Revenue` — $ booked for that month
- `RevPAR Index` — Rankbreeze's own index (use cautiously, breaks down at low market RevPAR)
- `Rental RevPAR`, `Rental RevPAR STLY`, `Rental RevPAR LY`
- `Market RevPAR`, `Market RevPAR STLY`, `Market RevPAR LY`
- `Occupancy %`, `Occupancy % STLY`, `Market Occupancy %`, `Market Occupancy % STLY`, `Occupancy % LY`, `Market Occupancy % LY`

**ADR is not in the export.** Compute it: `ADR = RevPAR / (Occupancy% / 100)`.

## Step 1: Read and inspect the file

Use pandas. Filter out empty rows. Quick sanity check:

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_excel('<file>')
df = df[df['Year & Month'].notna()].copy()
print(df['Group Name'].iloc[0])  # confirm listing name
```

## Step 2: Detect first-year status

This is critical. Check whether ALL of `Rental RevPAR STLY`, `Occupancy % STLY` are zero across all months.

```python
is_first_year = (df['Rental RevPAR STLY'].sum() == 0) and (df['Occupancy % STLY'].sum() == 0)
```

If first-year:
- Drop YoY/STLY framing entirely from the digest
- Note this explicitly: "First year on platform — no last-year comparison possible. Frame is listing vs market, current period."
- The current year IS the baseline being established

If not first-year:
- Use STLY columns for trend analysis
- Compare market trend (Market RevPAR vs Market RevPAR STLY) to assess whether the market is rising or falling
- Compare listing trend to market trend

## Step 3: Compute the comparisons

For every month with non-zero data, compute:

```python
df['Listing_ADR'] = df.apply(lambda r: r['Rental RevPAR']/(r['Occupancy %']/100) if r['Occupancy %']>0 else 0, axis=1)
df['Market_ADR']  = df.apply(lambda r: r['Market RevPAR']/(r['Market Occupancy %']/100) if r['Market Occupancy %']>0 else 0, axis=1)
df['RevPAR_vs_Market'] = df.apply(lambda r: r['Rental RevPAR']/r['Market RevPAR']-1 if r['Market RevPAR']>0 else None, axis=1)
df['Occ_vs_Market']    = df.apply(lambda r: (r['Occupancy %']-r['Market Occupancy %'])/r['Market Occupancy %'] if r['Market Occupancy %']>0 else None, axis=1)
df['ADR_vs_Market']    = df.apply(lambda r: r['Listing_ADR']/r['Market_ADR']-1 if r['Market_ADR']>0 else None, axis=1)
```

## Step 4: Identify the meaningful months

Not every month is comparable. Filter to "meaningful" months for the headline read:

- **Drop months with 0 listing revenue** (calendar blocks, not booked yet, or owner stays — not a strategy signal)
- **Drop months with very low Market RevPAR** (e.g., <$15) — index becomes unreliable. These are typically deep low-season months (Sep–Dec depending on market) where pacing is incomplete.
- The remaining months are the headline comparison set.

Compute averages across the meaningful months only:

```python
meaningful = df[(df['Rental Revenue'] > 0) & (df['Market RevPAR'] >= 15)].copy()
avg_revpar_premium = meaningful['RevPAR_vs_Market'].mean()
avg_adr_premium = meaningful['ADR_vs_Market'].mean()
total_revenue_meaningful = meaningful['Rental Revenue'].sum()
```

## Step 5: Write the digest

Structure the response as:

### Big picture (2–3 lines)
One sentence on the strategy result (RevPAR vs market). One sentence on the ADR/occupancy split. One caveat if relevant (first-year, missing STLY, market data thin in low season).

### Caveats
- First-year status if applicable
- STLY data missing if applicable
- Months excluded from the headline read and why

### Detail breakdown
- RevPAR vs market — month by month, with the standout months called out
- Occupancy vs market — frame as the deliberate tradeoff, not a problem
- ADR vs market — frame as the strategy executing
- Any month where RevPAR fell below market — diagnostic, but one month doesn't change the strategy

### Strategic framing
End with how to walk an owner through this if they're questioning strategy. The line: optimizing for occupancy would lower revenue. RevPAR is the real outcome.

**Style:** Big picture first, then concise bullet details — no walls of text. Match Fede's preferred tone.

## Step 6: Render the three-chart visualization

Use `visualize:show_widget` (load the `chart` module via `visualize:read_me` first if you haven't already this conversation).

The default visual is **three vertical bar charts stacked**, in this order:

1. **RevPAR: listing vs market** — purple (`#534AB7`) for listing, gray (`#B4B2A9`) for market
2. **ADR: listing vs market** — teal (`#1D9E75`) for listing, gray for market
3. **Occupancy: listing vs market** — coral (`#D85A30`) for listing, gray for market

Above the charts, place 3 metric cards:
- Avg RevPAR vs market (the headline win)
- Avg ADR vs market (the strategy executing)
- Revenue booked YTD across meaningful months

X-axis: only the meaningful months (skip empty/low-season months that would distort the read).

Tooltip and tick formatters: round to nearest dollar for RevPAR/ADR, nearest whole percent for occupancy.

Each canvas needs `role="img"` and `aria-label` per the visualize chart module rules.

## Step 7: Offer next steps

After the digest and chart, offer:
- A reduced single-chart version (just RevPAR) for owner-facing sharing if they only want one visual
- An owner-facing message draft if Fede signals the conversation is heading toward a strategy debate
- A polished owner-facing PDF report (see Step 8) if Fede signals he wants to send something formal

## Step 8: Owner-facing PDF report

When Fede asks for a PDF, a report, or "something I can send the owner," produce a polished 2–3 page PDF using `reportlab` for layout and `matplotlib` for the charts (saved as PNGs and embedded). This is the deliverable that goes to the homeowner, so the voice and framing differ from the internal digest above.

### Tone for owner-facing materials

The internal digest is for Fede — it can talk about strategy tradeoffs, proprietary pricing, etc. The owner-facing PDF cannot. Adjust:

- **Confirm the client type first** (Blackbird vs RevFactor — see the section above) and apply the matching scope rules. The PDF can be a Blackbird version (full-scope, "our listing" language ok) or a RevFactor version (revenue-only, no credit-claiming on reviews/listing/ops). The cover page and the takeaway are the two places where the language differs most visibly.
- **Don't preempt complaints the data doesn't justify.** If the listing is winning on both rate and occupancy this period, do NOT include lines like "the goal is total revenue, not booked nights" or "we trade occupancy for rate." Those read as defensive and signal weakness where there is none. Save that framing for periods where occupancy actually IS below market and the question is likely to come up.
- **Match the framing to the data.** When occupancy is below market → describe it as a deliberate strategy that trades a few occupancy points for a higher rate. When occupancy is above market → describe rate and occupancy as winning at the same time (a strong combination). Don't carry the "tradeoff" framing into months where there is no tradeoff to defend.
- **Define every term in plain language.** Owners don't necessarily know RevPAR or ADR. One short parenthetical or sentence per term is enough — e.g., "RevPAR (revenue per available night)".
- **Lead with what's actually winning.** RevPAR, ADR, then occupancy — same order as the internal digest — but every section header should describe the metric in owner-friendly terms ("the headline outcome", "your nightly rate vs the market", "nights booked vs the market").
- **Close confidently, not defensively.** The takeaway paragraph should describe what the listing is doing well and what's worth watching going forward. It should NOT justify the strategy. For RevFactor specifically, keep the takeaway focused on rate, occupancy, and revenue outcomes — don't generalize into operational compliments.

### Structure

1. **Header** — `Listing performance review` as H1, then a subtitle line: `<Listing name> · <Month range> · Prepared by <Blackbird | RevFactor>`. The "Prepared by" must match the client's business relationship; never label a RevFactor client's report as a Blackbird report or vice versa.
2. **Three metric cards** in a row — RevPAR vs market, ADR vs market, Revenue booked. Card background `#F7F6F1`, centered label + value. Color the RevPAR value in `#534AB7` (purple) and the ADR value in `#0F6E56` (teal); keep revenue in default ink.
3. **Big picture** — one paragraph (3–4 sentences) of plain-language summary. Lead with the comp-set result, end with the market-context framing if relevant.
4. **Three chart sections**, each: section heading, one-line definition of the metric, the bar chart, one-line caption with the numbers. Wrap each in `KeepTogether` so the heading/chart/caption never split across pages. Use the same color system as the widget: purple/teal/coral for the listing, gray (`#B4B2A9`) for market.
5. **Market context** — when there's enough LY/STLY data, two short paragraphs: first describing how the wider market has moved YoY, second describing how the listing held up against that backdrop. Skip this section entirely if data is too thin to read a market trend.
6. **Summary table** — all three months in columns, RevPAR / ADR / Occupancy / Revenue in rows, listing and market interleaved. Mark any still-pacing months with an asterisk and footnote that "Most stays are booked in the 30–60 days before arrival."
7. **The takeaway** — one short paragraph, confident voice. Describe what's working and what we're monitoring next. No strategy-defense language.
8. **Sources footer** — single small-text line: `Sources: Rankbreeze market data, comp set defined by Rankbreeze. RevPAR = revenue per available night. ADR = revenue ÷ booked nights. Occupancy = booked nights ÷ available nights.`

### Technical notes

- Render charts with matplotlib at `dpi=200`, figsize ~`(7.2, 3.2)`. Save as PNG to a working dir, then embed via `reportlab.platypus.Image` at `width=7.1*inch, height=3.0*inch`.
- Bar chart styling: hide top/right spines, light gray gridlines on y-axis only, value labels above each bar, legend in upper right (no frame). Format y-axis as `${int(v):,}` for dollars and `{int(v)}%` for occupancy.
- Use Letter page size, ~0.65" margins. Helvetica throughout — no need to load custom fonts.
- Wrap chart blocks (heading + intro + image + caption) in `KeepTogether`. This sometimes pushes a chart to the next page leaving whitespace below — that's the right tradeoff over stranded captions.
- **Do NOT use Unicode subscript/superscript characters** anywhere in the PDF — reportlab's built-in fonts don't include those glyphs and they render as black boxes. Use ReportLab's XML markup tags (`<sub>`, `<super>`) in `Paragraph` objects if needed.
- Save the PDF to the outputs directory with filename pattern `<ListingName>_Performance_Review_<Period>.pdf` (spaces → underscores).

### Verification before sharing

Before declaring the PDF done, render at least one page to an image (e.g., via `pdf2image.convert_from_path`) and inspect it. Watch for:
- Stranded captions or headings on the wrong page
- Black-box characters indicating missing glyphs
- Truncated chart titles or value labels
- Empty bottom-of-page whitespace large enough to be worth reflowing

## Things to avoid

- **Don't lean on RevPAR Index from Rankbreeze blindly.** When market RevPAR is very low (deep low season), the index returns absurd numbers (e.g., 2811% in December because market RevPAR is $5). Compute your own ratio and gate on a market RevPAR floor.
- **Don't frame lower occupancy as a problem.** It's the tradeoff. The strategy is RevPAR-optimized, not occupancy-optimized.
- **Don't engage in defending specific pricing decisions** (why a particular night was priced X). The strategy is proprietary IP. The conversation stays at outcome level: RevPAR, ADR, revenue.
- **Don't carry defensive framing into owner-facing materials when the data doesn't call for it.** Pre-empting a complaint the owner has no reason to raise reads as weakness. See Step 8 tone notes.
- **Don't compute YoY trend from `*_LY` columns unless they have data across multiple months.** Rankbreeze sometimes only populates LY for the last 3 months of the year, which is not enough to read a trend.
- **Don't reproduce the chart content as text after rendering it.** The widget shows the user; restating the bars in prose is redundant.

## Example trigger phrases

- "Owner wants feedback on their performance, here's the report"
- "Help me digest this listing review"
- "Can you look at this Rankbreeze export"
- "[uploads Listing_Review_*.xlsx with no other context]"
- "Client is questioning our pricing — here's their numbers"
- "Can you build a PDF report I can share with the owner?"
- "Turn this into something I can send the homeowner"


# Fede's voice — tone profile for client emails

*Distilled from sent owner-comms in Gmail: Hunt May Bookings, Leslie Nightly Rate Question, Abby Sharp Pricing Update, Kassidy Tucson Pricing Strategy, Joanna Property Analysis, Sarah/William Revenue Potential, Guatemala Owner Report. Add this as a "Step 9" section in the revfactor-listing-review SKILL.md so future email drafts match his voice.*

## Voice patterns he actually uses

- **Casual opener.** "Hi [Name]! How are you?" / "Hi Guys!" / "Hey [Name]!" Almost never a cold "Hello" or "Dear". If he's already in a thread, he skips the opener.
- **Smileys are normal.** ":)" lands naturally at the end of a friendly sentence. Don't force them, but don't strip them either.
- **"We" not "I"** when describing the work — "we've been reviewing the booking data", "we made some adjustments", "we're seeing". Singular only for personal notes ("I'm happy to walk through this on a call").
- **Specific raw numbers, always paired with the comparison.** "$7,504 on the books, a 27% increase from $5,900 last May" — not "performance is up". He shows the work.
- **Acronyms used naturally.** ADR, RevPAR, STLY, LY, occupancy — all comfortable. He occasionally defines them in passing for newer owners ("RevPAR (ADR/Occ)") but only the first time in a thread.
- **Pacing/strategy vocabulary that sounds like him**: "the books", "pace", "close the gap", "rate strength to work with", "premium capture window", "booking window", "rate-led month", "the expected trade as price moves up the curve", "yield high on prime bookings".
- **No em dashes or en dashes.** Use periods or commas instead. Parentheticals (like this) are fine for short asides, but break longer thoughts into separate sentences rather than stringing them with dashes. This applies everywhere: client emails, owner reports, even internal notes drafted in his voice.
- **Light typos and casual punctuation are fine.** Don't over-polish. He'll write "lol", "haha", a missed apostrophe, or "underperformaning". Keeping a small imperfection makes it sound real.
- **Honest hedges.** "We know this sounds risky and we're in uncharted territory" / "in any case happy to jump on a call". He admits uncertainty rather than over-promising.
- **Concrete commitments at the end.** "I'm happy to start making pricing adjustments today if you'd like" / "Let me know what you think" / "happy to walk through any of it on a call". He gives the owner a clear next step.
- **Reassurance close, often with a smiley.** "Just want to make sure you feel good about the plan and confident that we'll hit our revenue goals (and ideally beat them!)" / "we always aim to achieve higher results :)"
- **Sign-off**: "Federico" for more formal owner reports, "Fede" for warm threads with regular owners.

## Phrases to NOT use (sound like a consultant, not Fede)

- "On Bowman," / "On Pine Grove," as a paragraph opener — too clipped. He'd say "Bowman is doing X" or "For Pine Grove, ..."
- "The honest read" / "the data shows" / "directionally" — analyst voice.
- "I'd hold the current strategy" — passive and detached. He'd say "I'd give the strategy another 30 days" or "let's let it ride for 30 more days".
- "outran demand" / "the property absorbed" / "we pushed further than" — abstract. He'd say "we pushed rate a bit too aggressively" or "the rate move didn't get accepted".
- "Bottom line" / "key takeaway" — corporate.
- Bullet points in casual reply emails. Bullets are fine in structured analyses (Property Analysis, Owner Report). For replies to client concerns, he writes in flowing paragraphs.

## When the data is mixed (some listings winning, some losing)

Mirror the structure he used in the Leslie thread: acknowledge the owner's concern first, give the framework you're tracking against (current pace vs STLY vs LY, or vs market), share the specific numbers, then either defend the strategy with evidence OR own the miss and commit to a correction. Don't do the same thing for all listings in one email — adapt per listing.

## When admitting a miss (like Pine Grove)

He owns it directly but constructively. Pattern from "Pricing Update" thread with Abby: acknowledge → name the specific adjustment being made → give the framework being used to monitor → offer a call. Don't pad with apology language. One direct sentence + the fix + the monitoring plan is the right length.

## Reference snippets (real Fede)

**Casual + numbers + emoji close (Hunt May Bookings):**

> Hi Guys!
>
> Looks like we're closing May with $7504.38 on the books, which is a 27% increase from the $5900 from May 2024, with the booking we just got!
>
> We have 87% occupancy vs 57% market occupancy. Our RevPar (ADR/Occ) is $181.63 vs $139.41 Mkt, and occupancy in the market is 10% down from last year.
>
> Wanted to share this good news but it's too late to text, lol!
>
> I know June is coming slow still, but May's booking window was 10 days, which is a huge drop from last year, so we may expect to see lots of last minute!
>
> Thanks again for staying on top of our performance and want to make sure you know we're working hard on making this property profitable so you can get many more for us to manage :)
>
> Fede

**Defending strategy after owner pushback (Leslie Nightly Rate Question):**

> Hi Leslie! Thanks so much for your email — I really appreciate your insights to making sure we stay on track for our summer goals.
>
> To give you a transparent view into how we're tracking performance, we're actively monitoring a dashboard called "Summer 2025 FU" that compares three key indicators: Current Pace, Last Year (LY), and Same Time Last Year (STLY)...
>
> This tells us that market demand is currently stronger than last year at this point, up more than 7 points STLY — a very positive sign. Our current occupancy is behind, but we're also holding at a much higher ADR — up ~64% vs. STLY and ~69% vs. LY — which means we have rate strength to work with.
>
> We're currently in what we call the "premium capture window"...
>
> That said, I'm more than happy to start making pricing adjustments today if you'd like to begin moving the needle sooner. Just want to make sure you feel good about the plan and confident that we'll hit our revenue goals (and ideally beat them!).

**Acknowledging slow performance + small adjustment (Abby Sharp Pricing Update):**

> Hi Abby! How are you?
>
> We've been reviewing the booking data with Gaston, who supports me on Revenue Management, and made some adjustments to lower future rates slightly — this should help open up the booking window and align with your great suggestion.
>
> Looking at past data across Airbnb, VRBO, and upcoming bookings, March 2025 was slower compared to previous years. But we're optimistic that with the adjustments we've made, we're on track to close the gap with April and May...
>
> Hope you find this helpful, in any case would love to jump on a call to walk you through this data and chat more ideas :) Let me know when it's good!
>
> Federico

**Tight rate-led summary (Guatemala Owner Report):**

> April's report is attached.
>
> A rate-led month: net revenue closed at $3,241 — up 15.5% on April 2025, with ADR climbing 44% over the same period. Occupancy gave back about seven points as the season tapers, which is the expected trade as price moves up the curve.
>
> One operations item and a pricing observation flagged inside.
>
> Happy to walk through any of it on a call.
>
> — Federico
